1.pericope_label: Shall we continue in sin? Dead to sin, and baptized into his death

schools.summary: State the objection plainly, that if grace abounded where sin abounded it might seem best to continue in sin; charge those who imagine gratuitous righteousness given apart from newness of life with shamefully rending Christ asunder; observe that some take the denial for mere indignant reproof, whereas the Apostle commonly answers so even while carrying a long argument, rejecting the slander first by an indignant negative and then disproving it carefully; and hold it beyond any question that we put on Christ in baptism and are baptized for this very end, that we may be one with him.

Hear the opening as a debater's phrase and an echo of the rabbinical method of question and answer, and parse the verb as a deliberative subjunctive meaning to tarry; set the chapter in the argument's architecture, the previous chapters having handled justification by faith and this one passing to the second root idea, union with Christ, the one juridical and the other not; correct that are dead to that died and hold the strict aorist against the perfect, the single past act against the prolonged, the whole change being summed up in one moment; draw the argument from the fact as well as the tense, since the dead cannot act as if alive; and be most guarded about the sacrament, since rendering the preposition into would make union with Christ come to pass by means of baptism, which is not the Apostle's idea, baptism being the public proclamation of what has happened — while still glossing the phrase as incorporation into communion with Christ and into his mystical body.

Mark that the Apostle had earlier only denied the consequence and here removes its very foundation; protest at the translation of the denial, since the Greek means let it not be, by no means, far from it, and it is not proper to make the sacred name so familiar; take being baptized into Christ as receiving the doctrine of Christ crucified and taking baptism for proof of the genuineness of that faith and of the obligation to live by its precepts; and hold that in baptism we are through faith ingrafted into Christ and draw new spiritual life from this new root.

Note that the disavowal shows the inconsistency but that the Apostle is not content with a bare condemnation and proceeds to treat the subject another way; turn the argument back on the objector in one sentence, that he has renounced sin, become dead to it and been buried with Christ, so that he cannot possibly admit the same sin again; and deny that baptism is merely the grace of remission or even of adoption, as the earlier baptism conferred remission only, since while it purges sins and ministers the gift of the Spirit it is also the counterpart of the sufferings of Christ.

Add the warning the argument invites, that unholy professors may have had the outward sign of a death unto sin and a new birth unto righteousness and yet never have passed from the family of Satan to that of God.

debates: Whether the abounding of grace gives any ground for continuing in sin.
How the Apostle's denial should be rendered.
What the tense of the verb rendered dead requires.
What baptism effects, and whether union with Christ comes about by means of it.
outliers: Ellicott alone describes the chapter as the turn from the first root idea of the system to the second.
Clarke alone objects to the English rendering of the denial as making the sacred name too familiar.
Robertson alone denies that union with Christ is brought to pass by means of baptism.
Cyril alone contrasts this baptism with the earlier one that conferred remission only.
Theodoret alone answers the whole objection by a single question put back to the objector.

4.pericope_label: Buried with him by baptism: planted together, and the old man crucified

schools.summary: Call the burial a manifest reference to the ancient and only way of administering the ordinance, by dipping, when a person is covered in water as a corpse with earth; put the transition as a knot, the Apostle passing from a fellowship in death to a fellowship in life, the two joined indissolubly; press the grafting hardest, that it designates not a conformity of example but a secret union by which we are joined to Christ, who reviving us by his Spirit transfers his own virtue to us, the graft having life or death in common with its tree; take the old man for the corruption of nature, called a man because it dwells in us and rules and has its several members, and called old because it is the poison of the old serpent; or else refer the epithet not to age but to relation, as the Old Testament is old with reference to the New, the old man beginning to be old only when a commencing regeneration destroys him by degrees, and identify him with the whole nature we bring from the womb.

Note the allusion to the ancient manner of baptizing in a phrase, or draw the picture out, the whole body put under so that the man seems drowned and dead and rising seems to have a resurrection to life; report that our translation does not express the sense of the plants meant, which grow the one upon and in the other and draw sap from it, as the mistletoe on the oak or the scion on its stock; make the old man coeval with our being and as old as the fall;.

Grant that immersion is the idea which would strike the great mass of unprejudiced readers, and that it cannot be proved beyond objection, while insisting that the Apostle's main scope lay elsewhere; take the word for planted together, which occurs nowhere else, as meaning sown at the same time, so that the figure is of grain springing up together; or else derive the adjective from the verb to grow together, and say the metaphor is of parasitic growth applied to natural growth, a bud or graft reckoned as part of the stock it is set in; read the burial structurally, as the seal upon death showing no revival possible and the one step separating death from resurrection; take the old self for that congeries of evil habits acquired in heathenism, killed ideally if not actually in baptism — or object that this took place not at baptism but was only pictured there, having happened when we died to sin.

Say that the sacrament itself has taught us to fly from sin, since it carries in it the representation of the Lord's death, and find the resurrection already in the change of word, since whatever is planted springs up again; read the verse against those who would make the sufferings apparent only, since whatever Christ endured for us he suffered in reality and not in appearance and we are made partakers of it; deny that the old man is our nature, since it is our evil inclination that is so called; and stand back from the verse to describe the epistle, in which the Apostle continually digresses into exhortation instead of dividing the letter as he does elsewhere, doctrine first and moral instruction after, blending the second with the subject throughout so as to gain it an easy admission.

debates: Whether the burial alludes to immersion, and whether that is the Apostle's point.
Whether planted together means sown at the same time or grafted into.
Why the old man is called old.
Whether the old man is our nature or our evil inclination, and when he was crucified.
outliers: Chrysostom alone contrasts the structure of this epistle with the Apostle's others.
Barnes alone takes the word to mean sown at the same time rather than grown into.
Barnes alone concedes the allusion to immersion while denying that it is the Apostle's scope.
Theodoret alone insists that not our nature but our evil inclination is meant by the old man.
Robertson alone holds that the crucifixion of the old man took place not at baptism but was only pictured there.

7.pericope_label: He that is dead is freed from sin: Christ dieth no more

schools.summary: Take the word for the one elsewhere rendered justified, glossing it absolved, since the dead man is no longer liable to have the charge of sin brought against him, and parse it as a perfect, so that he stands justified; set the verse out as a piece of formal reasoning, the general proposition adduced to prove the particular one that the ethically dead man is no longer sin's slave; take the sentence also for a proverb and report a rabbinic saying to match, that the dead man is free from commands; read the once-dying as sufficiency, no other atonement being needed since the one made is enough for all; turn the same fact into a controversy against the sacrificial character of the mass; and make the eternal subsistence of Christ's life the guarantee of the permanence of our own, since were that life to fail the whole fabric faith builds on it would fall to the ground.

Ground the argument on what death does rather than on what the word means, since if death destroys all the actions of life we who died to sin ought to cease from the actions sin exercised while it lived, the word meaning freed or reclaimed from bondage as a man is freed from a charge when a judge absolves him; fence off the wrong death, since a natural death is the effect of sin and inflicted as punishment, and so far from being an atonement that many who die in their sins will rise in them; head off the implication that death once ruled over Christ, who in giving himself up did in a manner surrender to its power, but so that it was impossible he should be held bound by its pangs, submitting to its dominion only as it were for a moment; support the resurrection as well attested, foretold by the prophets and by Christ, affirmed by angels, witnessed by the apostles and the Spirit.

Start from the literal rendering and travel further, asking whether it does not mean that the man who has received Christ by faith and been made partaker of the Spirit has had his old man and all his evil propensities destroyed, so that he is not merely justified from sin but delivered from it; divide it in two, freedom from the guilt of past and from the power of present sin, as dead men are free from their former masters' commands; and make it an exhortation, that if we are risen with Christ we should seek the things above and set our affections there, since sin has no more dominion over the man who walks in humble obedience to an indwelling Christ.

Need no proverb, but ask who ever yet saw a dead man invading another's marriage-bed, or imbruing his hands in bloodshed, or committing any other item in the catalogue of iniquities; and add the posture the argument requires, that having been buried with Christ we should be dead indeed unto sin and await the resurrection.

debates: How much the word rendered freed contains — absolution, justification, or deliverance from sin's power.
Whether the death in view is natural or ethical.
Whether death ever had dominion over Christ.
What follows from the fact that he dies no more.
outliers: Gill alone denies that a natural death is meant, and alone rejects the notion that dying atones for sin.
Barnes alone finds a rabbinic proverb standing behind the sentence.
Theodoret alone argues the point from the plain impossibility of a corpse sinning.
Robertson alone draws a confessional conclusion from the once-for-all death.
Ellicott alone sets the verse out as the major premise of a syllogism.
Calvin alone qualifies the implication that death ruled over Christ.

10.pericope_label: He died unto sin once: reckon yourselves dead, and let not sin reign

schools.summary: Quote a Latin commentator who renders the clause that Christ died on account of sin, once, and by a wretched death, taking the dative for the expiation of sins, and who warns that men die to sin in one way and Christ in another, the Apostle being fond of parallelism, in interpreting which much caution is needed; compress the sense into four words, to atone for and abolish it; set the two halves against their pattern, to die as truly unto sin as he died for sin and live as truly unto God as he lives with God; and call the clause about sin's rule a personification, sin being a king or tyrant who holds the desires of the mind and the members of the body under his control and governs the body by working on the passions.

Warn that having applied the freedom from death to our freedom from sin's tyranny we must still observe what is suitable to Christ in this form of speech, and supply at the next verse a definition of the analogy; mark that the Apostle does not stop at the mortifying but adds the living, since we die while living whenever we renounce sin; concede the residue while denying it the throne, since though sin dwells in us it is not to be so vigorous as to exercise a reigning power, the power of sanctification being superior to it; and guard the exhortation from the inference that it supposes any natural power of free will, being addressed to persons who had the Spirit.

Take the clause simply of design, that the death had respect to sin and was meant to destroy it and make atonement for it; fix the adverb as meaning once and once only, not once upon a time; make it the last sacrifice Christ made to sin, one that freed him from its dominion for ever and could not be repeated; call the exhortation the theoretical application to the readers, who are to regard themselves as insensible and inaccessible to sin but living in close allegiance to God; make the deadness as complete as that of the dead in their graves toward the things of this world; take the imperative as complete proof that baptism does not make a man dead to sin and alive to God, that being a spiritual operation only pictured there, so that the verse is a plea to live up to the ideal of the baptized life; and read the epithet mortal as at variance with the immortal life just described, or as subject to death, self-indulgence being inconsistent with trust in a vicarious atonement.

Draw from the singleness of the death the singleness of the sacrament, since he who died once and cannot die again, possessing now an immortal body, gives us one baptism and no second; demand that the body be displayed dead to the inworking of sin while embracing the life that is after Christ; distinguish a reign from a tyranny, the one exercised over consenting subjects and the other over those who submit unwillingly, so that the exhortation is to stop agreeing to sin's government, its reign having been overthrown by the incarnation; and come at the verse through the petition of the Lord's Prayer, since he who has cleansed himself in deed and thought and word can say with boldness, thy kingdom come.
Enter the qualification that since unholy lusts are not quite rooted out in this life it must be the Christian's care to resist their motions and strive earnestly against them.

debates: In what sense Christ died unto sin, and how far the parallel with our dying may be pressed.
What the command to reckon requires, and whether baptism effects what it describes.
Whether the rule of sin is properly a reign or a tyranny.
Why the body is called mortal at this point.
outliers: Clarke alone quotes a warning that the Apostle's parallelisms need caution in interpretation.
Theodoret alone distinguishes reign from tyranny by the consent of the governed, and alone infers one baptism from the one death.
Robertson alone insists again that the change is a spiritual operation only pictured in baptism.
Gill alone guards against inferring a natural power of free will from the exhortation.
Cyril alone reads the verse through a petition of the Lord's Prayer.

13.pericope_label: Yield not your members as weapons of unrighteousness: not under law but under grace

schools.summary: Insist that the word means not instruments but arms or weapons which sin is to wield, and carry the military figure to the end of the chapter, where the wages of sin is the soldier's pay; or let the word out again as an old term for tools of any kind, of shop or war, and press instead the tense of the prohibition, which forbids a habit; take the members for those of the body, the hands, the feet, the tongue, as a specification of what the previous verse covered by the general word body; read the promise as at once a statement that sin ought not to rule and a conviction that it will not, or say only that it shall not lord it over us even if not yet wholly dead; and show that the second objection is not the first, the verb here being an aorist and asking about occasional acts where the opening verb was a present and asked about continuing in a life of sin, the answer being couched under a different metaphor, freedom from the one and service to the other.

Take the members for the several powers and faculties of the soul, citing a version that renders the word simply your souls; grant that sin remains after conversion and has great power to hinder what is good and effect what is evil, so that it seems as though it would regain its dominion; dismiss without ceremony the expositions that have little or no appearance of truth and give as the most probable that the letter of the law is meant, which cannot renovate the soul, against the grace of the Spirit by which we are renewed; and explain why the objection had to be anticipated, since the wisdom of the flesh is ever clamorous against the mysteries of God, men supposing that when the law is removed as the rule of life all discipline falls to the ground.

Draw a rule of conscience that nobody else states, that it is no sin to be tempted and the sin lies in the yielding, since while it exists only in the solicitation it is the devil's sin and not ours; describe the law as that which exacts obedience without giving power to obey and condemns every transgression without providing for its removal, and call it a dispensation of terror and bondage which shows sin without enabling us to conquer it, grace being the merciful dispensation that brings complete victory; add that if a man becomes subject to sin again it will be the effect of his own choice or negligence.

Tie the weapons back to the reign already spoken of, mentioning in strict keeping with it the artillery of that reign and teaching the way of victory, since the weapons sin uses against us are our own members; say that nature no longer fights singly but has the grace of the Spirit for her assistant, the law before grace having taught only what was to be done and afforded no help to those who would do it; and report the method, that the objection is noted because of the gainsayers, first reprobated by pointing out its absurdity and only then answered at length.

debates: Whether the members are the organs of the body or the faculties of the soul.
Whether the word means weapons specifically or tools of any kind.
What law it is that believers are said not to be under.
How the objection raised here differs from the one raised at the opening of the chapter.
outliers: Clarke alone distinguishes temptation from consent, making the sin the devil's until we yield.
Gill alone takes the members for the faculties of the soul rather than the organs of the body.
Ellicott alone carries the military figure through to the wages at the close of the chapter.
Robertson alone distinguishes the aorist here from the present at the opening, single acts against a life of sin.
Calvin alone dismisses the rival expositions summarily before offering his own.

16.pericope_label: His servants ye are whom ye obey: the mould of doctrine, and freedom from sin

schools.summary: Find a doctrine in the apparent tautology, that what you make yourselves you become, the habit you form ending as your second nature; draw the argument from the readers' own experience; find the fault in the English, since there is no whereas in the Greek and the verb is an imperfect, so that the gratitude is not for their having been slaves of sin but for their turning from it; take the figure of slavery as the answer to the question just raised, slaves being slaves of the one they obey whatever their profession; refuse the metal and make the phrase a pattern of teaching, an express moral rule of life to whose direction they were handed over; deny that anything lies between the two services, since we have simply changed masters and there is no no-man's-land in this warfare; and answer the paradox with the liturgical phrase that this is a service which is perfect freedom.

Deny that the Apostle can be thanking God that these men had been servants of sin, than which nothing is more disagreeable to him, and say that the thanks are for their being now free of that drudgery; insist that the preceding denial was no bare expression of abhorrence, a confutation following at once from the contrary supposition, since the yoke of Christ and that of sin are so contrary that no one can bear both; explain that the thanksgiving stands there to teach that the change came not by their own merit but by the special mercy of God; enumerate what the freedom is not — not from a sinful nature, a corrupt heart, vain thoughts, sinful words, or sinful actions altogether, but from the damning power of sin, the sentence having been executed on Christ instead; and argue from the unreasonableness of the thing, that a man made free ought to maintain his freedom and should not be brought again under a dominion he has been released from.

Put the alternative plainly, that sin is the service of Satan and righteousness the service of Christ; re-point the sentence so that it reads, thanks be to God that although ye were the servants of sin, nevertheless ye have obeyed from the heart; read the word for what they were delivered into as a mould, and press the figure hardest, since our minds being pliant and ductile should be conformed to the gospel precepts as liquid metal takes the figure of the mould it is poured into; take the verb for freedom as the technical term for the manumission of a slave and find here a second personification, sin and righteousness both being made persons; and set out the whole method of the argument to this point in a numbered table, from bondage to sin through the knowledge of sin by the law to the revelation of righteousness in the gospel and the faith that embraces it.

Say that it is not possible to obey two lords at once; take the thanksgiving as pointing out the change; and put the conclusion in one line, that having cast away the slavery of sin and taken the yoke of righteousness a man cannot bear the latter and obey the former.
State the rule flatly, that every man is the servant of the master to whose commands he yields himself, and say that they were delivered into the gospel as into a mould.

debates: Whether the thanksgiving can be for their having been servants of sin.
Whether the form of doctrine is a mould they were cast in or a pattern they were handed over to.
What being made free from sin does and does not include.
Whether any middle state lies between the two services.
outliers: Ellicott alone reads the apparent tautology as the doctrine of habit becoming second nature.
Clarke alone re-points the sentence to make the thanksgiving concessive.
Gill alone enumerates what the freedom is not, restricting it to the damning power of sin.
Robertson alone denies that any middle ground lies between the two servitudes.
Wesley alone sets out the whole argument of the epistle to this point as a numbered table.

19.pericope_label: I speak after the manner of men: the two servitudes and their fruit

schools.summary: Refer the apology not to the manner of speech but to the severity of the demand, since having required great strictness of life the Apostle seemed to be saying something burdensome and too much for human nature, and speaks so to show he makes no exorbitant demand; say that the exhortation is suited to their nature, the speaker being well aware of the passions that contend in a mortal body; put the asymmetry from the other end, that they fulfilled the precepts of sin only and did not receive the laws of righteousness at all; and make the silence itself the answer about fruit, since they confess its injury by saying nothing, and however barefaced a man may be he cannot but feel shame once the enjoyment is over.

Make the apology narrower still, a begging of pardon for using the word slaving in connection with righteousness, though it is a good word for a time when self-assertiveness and personal liberty bulk so large in modern speech; make the infirmity intellectual, the dulness of their understanding, so that the mystical phrase used just before might have been beyond them where this figure is clear even to a preoccupied mind; or make it moral, the word meaning weakness as opposed to vigour and the flesh often denoting the corrupt passions; make being free from righteousness a strong expression of total depravity that proves they had no native goodness, or keep it light, that they wore no collar of righteousness but did as they pleased; have them holding ashes in their hands now; and attend to the pointing, reporting that some place the question earlier, though the received construction is probably best.

Take the phrase for a known idiom of the Greek writers meaning what was easy to be comprehended, level with common understandings and delivered in a popular style, as distinct from the high flights of the poets and the studied obscurity of the philosophers; deny any third possibility, since if we cannot serve God and Mammon we cannot serve Christ and Satan, and quote a verse thought well meant and mistaken in which a man professes himself equally bent to good and evil and so both a devil and a saint; turn the argument into a claim, that they ought now to be as uniform and zealous in serving God as they once were in serving the devil.

Distinguish substance from manner, the accommodation being only in the manner, as when the Lord announced earthly things while speaking of heavenly mysteries, accommodating himself to an ignorant people; say simply that what was to be said was delivered in a way suited to their understandings; repeat the contrariety, that sin and righteousness are so opposed that a man who devotes himself to the one necessarily departs from the other, the two being set apart so that we may see each more clearly; ask what it would profit a man to amass the riches of the Indies or gain the whole world if his soul were lost by it; and admire the method, that the Apostle could not more strikingly have expressed his meaning than by appealing to their conscience and confessing the shame as it were in their own person.

Refuse the name of fruit to the pleasure and profit of sin, since sinners are but ploughing iniquity, sowing vanity and reaping the same, and observe that shame came into the world with sin and is still its certain effect.

debates: What the Apostle apologises for — the figure he uses, the plainness of his style, or the severity of his demand.
Whether the infirmity of the flesh is dulness of understanding or corruption of the passions.
Whether any man can stand between the two services.
How the question about fruit should be pointed.
outliers: Chrysostom alone refers the apology to the severity of the demand rather than to the manner of speech.
Robertson alone makes it an apology for applying the language of slavery to righteousness, and alone remarks on modern speech.
Clarke alone quotes and rejects a verse claiming that a man may be both devil and saint.
Ellicott alone reports an alternative pointing of the question about fruit.
Barnes alone reads freedom from righteousness as a proof of total depravity.

22.pericope_label: The fruit unto holiness, and the wages of sin against the gift of God

schools.summary: Count the antithesis in threes, God opposed to sin, holiness to shame, and life everlasting to everlasting death; and read the word for wages as the last term of a single figure running through the chapter, since sin has been said to reign and then to tyrannize, its weapons have been called our own badly disposed members, and the reward it pays is consistently called a soldier's wages, which is how the Apostle names military pay elsewhere; or take the closing phrase for a text of its own, observing that many are the proofs concerning the life eternal and that the Scriptures themselves suggest the ways of gaining it, declaring at one time that it is by faith.

Make the parallel from the other side, that as a twofold end of sin was mentioned before so now a twofold end of righteousness, sin bringing in this life the torments of an accusing conscience and in the next eternal death, while we now gather holiness as the fruit of righteousness and hope hereafter for eternal life; report the reading that makes the comparison disparaging, an allowance of meat doled out to sinners, but prefer that the Apostle is indirectly condemning the blind appetites of those whom sin ruinously allures; and take the death of every sin, original and actual, lesser and greater, as a corporeal death owing neither to the original constitution of men nor merely to divine appointment but to sin and to the decree of God on account of it.

Turn the two states into a chiasm, since as being free from righteousness is the finished character of a sinner, so being made free from sin is the finished character of a genuine Christian; mean by the death the second death and everlasting perdition, and turn the earning into a reproach, since every sinner earns it by long and painful service and divine justice would be in his debt if it did not pay him his due; or refuse to choose and take the death as temporal, spiritual and eternal at once; call the difference at the close remarkable, that evil works merit the reward they receive and good works do not, the former demanding wages where the latter accept a gift, so that a man may merit hell but cannot merit heaven.

State plainly that they are no longer without fruit, and mark the exact correspondence with the earlier verse; find the asymmetry in the grammar, eternal life standing in the accusative as object of the verb where the death set against it stood in the nominative; take the word for wages back to what is bought to be eaten with bread and thence to the pay of the Roman soldier, since it was once the custom to pay soldiers in such things, so that it means what a man earns or deserves, adding that sin pays its wages in full and takes no cut; and state the point of the broken antithesis, that the natural opposite would be wages again but is inappropriate here, so the free gift is substituted, since in spite of all their sanctification they will still not have earned eternal life, which is God's gift and not wages.

debates: What the word rendered wages properly means.
What death is owed — the corporeal, the second, or all three at once.
Why the Apostle breaks the antithesis and says gift where wages was expected.
Whether the imagery of the chapter is one sustained figure.
outliers: Theodoret alone traces the reign, the weapons and the wages as a single figure running through the chapter.
Barnes alone derives the word from the rations eaten with bread before it meant a soldier's pay.
Calvin alone reports and then sets aside the reading that makes it a disparaging allowance of meat.
Robertson alone notices that the two nouns stand in different cases.
Cyril alone turns the closing phrase into a survey of the ways the Scriptures assign for gaining eternal life.
